sections.heading: Have Plinth posted to you
sections.text: Print and web, forty pounds a year. Cancel whenever you like.

sections.heading: A magazine about buildings, for the people who live near them
sections.text: We started in 2019 with one question: why do the buildings we love and the buildings we get feel like different subjects?
sections.text2: Fourteen issues on, we still do not know. But we have got better at asking the people who might.

posts.title: The house that refused a front door
posts.text:
On a hill above the harbour there is a white house with no front door. There is a side door, and a back door, and a hatch for the coal that has not been used since 1971.

The owner says a front door is a promise to the street that she never wanted to make. We walked around it three times and found we agreed.

posts.title: What the curve knows
posts.text:
Stand under the facade at ten in the morning and the curve does something a flat wall cannot: it shows you where the light is going next.

The engineer who built it says the curve was cheaper than the argument about not having one.

posts.title: A harbour town, from above
posts.text:
The town was built by people who did not expect to be looked at from the cliff. That is why it works from the cliff.

Nothing lines up. Everything fits.

posts.title: First light, empty beach, no plan
posts.text:
We went to photograph a pier and the pier had gone. What was left was the beach, the light and a plan that no longer applied.

This is a story about the second plan.

posts.title: The villa as an argument
posts.text:
Every glass wall is a claim about who gets to look at whom. We spent a week in one and came out arguing with it.

The villa won most of the arguments. This is the one it lost.

posts.title: Salt water, close up
posts.text:
A wave is a building that lasts a second. We asked a structural engineer to explain one and she asked for a week.

She came back with a drawing and an apology.

posts.title: The architect who stopped drawing
posts.text:
Mara Voss has not drawn a building since 2019. Her practice has built eleven.

“I stopped when I noticed the drawings were winning,” she says. We asked what that meant. It took the whole afternoon.

posts.title: A laugh in the atrium
posts.text:
Acousticians measure atriums by clapping. We measured one by laughing, which turns out to be the more honest instrument.

It held the laugh for four seconds. The clap, for two.
